title: Who Is Responsible for HVAC in a Commercial Lease?
h1: Who Is Responsible for the HVAC System in a Commercial Lease?
description: In a commercial lease, HVAC duties depend on the lease type and its wording. See how landlords and tenants usually split maintenance, repair and replacement.
quick_answer: It depends on the lease. In gross leases, the landlord usually handles HVAC. In triple net leases, the tenant often pays for maintenance and repairs, and sometimes replacement. Many leases split it: the tenant covers routine service and the landlord covers major repairs or replacement. The lease language is what decides it.
body:
HVAC is one of the most common sources of friction between commercial landlords and tenants. Rooftop units, split systems and ductwork are expensive, and when a unit fails in the middle of a hot inland summer, nobody wants to argue about who pays. The best time to sort it out is before signing.

We service commercial HVAC for property owners and tenants across San Diego County and Orange County. We're not attorneys, and this isn't legal advice, but here's what we see in practice and what to look for in your lease.

How does the lease type affect HVAC responsibility?

Lease typeWho usually handles HVAC
Gross or full-service leaseThe landlord maintains and repairs the system, with costs built into rent.
Modified gross leaseOften split. The tenant may handle routine service while the landlord covers major repairs and replacement.
Single or double net leaseVaries widely. Read the maintenance and repair sections closely.
Triple net (NNN) leaseThe tenant often pays for maintenance and repairs, and some leases also make the tenant responsible for replacement.

These are general patterns. Two leases with the same label can say very different things, so the actual wording always controls.

What's the difference between maintenance, repair and replacement?

Most disputes come down to these three words:

  • Maintenance is routine care: filter changes, coil cleaning, belt checks, drain line clearing and scheduled inspections.
  • Repair fixes something that broke: a failed capacitor, a motor, a refrigerant leak or a control board.
  • Replacement means swapping out a unit or major component, such as a compressor or an entire rooftop unit.

A common setup is for the tenant to handle maintenance, both sides to share or cap repair costs, and the landlord to handle replacement as a capital expense. Some leases cap the tenant's yearly repair spend and shift anything above that to the landlord.

What should a tenant look for before signing?

Read the HVAC language carefully and ask questions about:

  1. Which units serve your space, and whether any are shared with other tenants.
  2. The age and condition of the equipment. Ask for service records.
  3. Whether you must keep a maintenance contract, and with whom.
  4. Who pays for repairs and whether there's a yearly cap.
  5. Who pays if a unit needs to be replaced, especially late in the lease term.
  6. How fast repairs must be made and what happens if the space becomes unusable.

Before signing, it's smart to have a technician inspect the units. A pre-lease inspection gives you a record of the system's condition on day one.

What should a landlord include in the lease?

Landlords benefit from clear terms too. Spell out the required maintenance schedule, who chooses the service company, how records are shared and how access to the roof or mechanical rooms works. Requiring documented maintenance protects the equipment and makes it easier to show whether a failure came from neglect or normal wear.

Why does regular maintenance matter for both sides?

Commercial systems often run long hours. Rooftop units in our area take a beating from summer heat, salt air near the coast and dust during Santa Ana winds. Skipped maintenance leads to clogged coils, worn belts and failed parts, and those failures tend to land on the hottest days.

Regular service keeps the system running more efficiently, gives early warning of bigger problems and creates a paper trail. That record is useful in any disagreement about responsibility.

What should happen when something breaks?

Follow the notice process in your lease. Tenants should report problems in writing to the landlord or property manager right away, even if they plan to call for service themselves. Landlords should respond quickly and keep tenants updated.

Keep copies of invoices, service reports and photos. If responsibility is unclear, a technician's written findings about the cause of the failure can help both parties sort it out.

Our commercial HVAC team handles inspections, maintenance plans and repairs for offices, retail spaces, restaurants and other commercial properties. We can also provide detailed service reports for landlords and tenants.
faqs: Does a tenant have to replace a broken HVAC unit?

Only if the lease says so. Some triple net leases put replacement on the tenant, while many others treat it as a landlord capital expense. Read the repair and replacement sections, and talk to a real estate attorney if the wording is unclear.
Who pays for HVAC maintenance in a triple net lease?

In most triple net leases, the tenant pays for routine maintenance, either directly or through common area charges. Many of these leases also require the tenant to keep a regular service contract and share the records.
What if the landlord won’t fix the HVAC?

Notify the landlord in writing and follow the lease's notice and repair terms. Keep records of the problem and any service reports. For legal options, talk to a real estate attorney before withholding rent or making repairs yourself.
Should I get an HVAC inspection before signing a commercial lease?

Yes. An inspection shows the age and condition of the equipment and flags problems before they become your responsibility. It also documents the system's condition at move-in, which helps if questions come up later.
